deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This is a 14 March 1813 observing log from Göttingen, made with the Reichenbach repeating circle. The purpose is to determine the latitude (Polhöhe) of the new observatory. Two methods are used: (A) lower culmination of a circumpolar star, and (B) off-meridian zenith distances of Polaris. The sidereal clock is fast by 6m47.5s ('Uhr voraus 6'47"5'). Barometer 28 Zoll 0.5 Linien (Paris); thermometer −6.0 (presumably Réaumur).

(1) RAW DATA.
- Star 1 (β Cephei; see corrections): 2 repetitions at clock times 9h40m11s and 9h47m26s. The circle starts at 0 and ends at 117°22'16.75". The mean zenith distance is ζ = 117°22'16.75"/2 = 58°41'8.37".
- α UMi: 4 repetitions at 10h0m29s, 10h4m31s, 10h10m7s and 10h18m3s. The total is 158°46'55", so the mean is 39°41'43.75". That mean is used on the next page.

(2) APPARENT PLACES. Mean place, then two corrections (precession/nutation and aberration type), then the apparent place.
- β Cep, right ascension in arc: α = 321°32'56.48" − 45.65" + 12.15" = 321°32'22.98". In time this is 21h26m9.5s.
- β Cep, declination: δ = 69°44'30.38" − 11.96" + 0.67" = 69°44'19.09".
- Lower culmination falls at sidereal time α+12h = 9h26m9.5s. On the fast clock that is 9h26m9.5s + 6m47.5s = 9h32m57s ('C.Z.' = Culminationszeit).
- α UMi, right ascension: 13°49'11.50" − 9'51.40" + 3'5.43" = 13°42'25.53", i.e. 0h54m49.7s.
- α UMi, declination: 88°18'41.66" + 6.26" − 6.39" = 88°18'41.53".
- Upper culmination of α UMi on the clock: 0h54m49.7s + 6m47.5s = 1h1m37.2s.

(3) REFRACTION (logarithms).
- 1.9805 is log of the mean refraction at about 58°41' (≈95.6").
- 1.6848 is log of the mean refraction at about 39°42' (≈48.4").
- 0.0291 is the common log factor for barometer and thermometer.
- So the refraction for β Cep is 10^(1.9805+0.0291) = 102.2" = 1'42.23".
- For Polaris (used on the next page) it is 10^(1.6848+0.0291) = 51.75".

(4) REDUCTION TO THE MERIDIAN (β Cep, lower culmination).
- Hour angles from C.Z.: t1 = 7m14s and t2 = 14m29s.
- Tabulated values 2 sin²(t/2)/sin1" are 102.7" and 411.8"; their sum is 514.5.
- The factor is cos φ cos δ / sin(φ+δ). Logs: log cos δ = 9.53946, log cos φ = 9.79385, log cosec(φ+δ) = 0.06812. These sum to 9.40143.
- Adding log 514.5 = 2.71139 gives 2.11282, i.e. 129.7". Dividing by the 2 observations gives +64.83" = +1'4.83".
- The sign is + because, below the pole, the meridian zenith distance is a maximum. In modern form (my statement): ζ_mer = ζ + (cos φ cos δ / sin(φ+δ)) · mean[2 sin²(t/2)].

(5) LATITUDE FROM β Cep.
- ζ_mer = 58°41'8.37" + 1'42.23" + 1'4.83" = 58°43'55.43" ('Merid. Z. D.').
- At lower culmination, ζ = 180° − φ − δ. So φ = 180° − (58°43'55.43" + 69°44'19.09") = 180° − 128°28'14.52" = 51°31'45.48" (Polhöhe).

(6) POLARIS, METHOD B.
- Hour angles: h = T − 1h1m37.2s, giving 8h58m51.8s, 9h2m53.8s, 9h8m29.8s and 9h16m25.8s. In arc these are 134°42'57", 135°43'27", 137°7'27" and 139°6'27" (near lower culmination).
- The zenith distance is computed from the half-angle form of the cosine rule: sin²(ζ/2) = sin²((δ−φ)/2) cos²(h/2) + cos²((δ+φ)/2) sin²(h/2).
- Gauss assumes φ = 51°31'54" and uses δ = 88°18'41.53". Then (δ−φ)/2 = 18°23'23.76" and (δ+φ)/2 = 69°55'17.76".
- Column 1: log sin 18°23'23.76" = 9.4989750.
- Next, log cos(h/2) for the four h: 9.5854306, 9.5762574, 9.5628789, 9.5432340.
- Column 2: log cos 69°55'17.76" = 9.5356810.
- Next, log sin(h/2) for the four h: 9.9651675, 9.9667420, 9.9688630, 9.9717397.
- Continued on the next page: the products are added, giving computed ζ. Their mean, 39°42'38.07", is compared with observed + refraction = 39°42'35.50". The difference corresponds to −0.999 dφ, giving φ = 51°31'56.57".
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All sums, the RA arc-to-time conversions, the culmination clock times, the hour angles and the 2 sin²(t/2) values check.
log cos φ = 9.79385 matches φ ≈ 51°31'54" (the provisional value) rather than the final 45.48". This is a negligible effect (≈0.00003 in the log).
The reduction to the meridian keeps only the first-order term. This is adequate at t ≤ 15 min. The clock rate is ignored (assumed sidereal and steady).
The two methods disagree by about 11": 45.5" from β Cep versus 56.6" from Polaris. The next night's β Cep gives 56.2", so the 14 March β Cep value is the outlier (observational, not computational).

results.what: Latitude of Göttingen from the lower-culmination zenith distance of β Cephei, reduced to the meridian with factor cosφcosδ/sin(φ+δ)·2sin²(t/2)/sin1"
results.modern_name: Circummeridian (Zirkummeridian) zenith-distance reduction; latitude by lower culmination of a circumpolar star

results.what: Half-angle form of the spherical cosine rule, sin²(ζ/2)=sin²((δ−φ)/2)cos²(h/2)+cos²((δ+φ)/2)sin²(h/2), used for logarithmic computation of Polaris's zenith distance
results.modern_name: Haversine-type form of the cosine law in spherical trigonometry
results.usually_credited_to: Classical spherical trigonometry (Euler/Lagrange-era identities); a 'haversine formula' standard in navigation

results.what: Latitude by off-meridian Polaris zenith distances with differential correction dφ
results.modern_name: Latitude by Polaris at any hour angle (differential correction)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard practice; Gauss's Göttingen latitude determinations 1813 are documented

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine observing and reduction log for Göttingen's latitude with the Reichenbach circle in 1813. The methods are standard, and Gauss's latitude work is well known. The only mildly interesting feature is the use of the half-angle cosine-rule form for logarithmic computation.

checkable.asserts: The half-angle formula is equivalent to cos ζ = sinφ sinδ + cosφ cosδ cos h (result 0).
The RA of Polaris in time is 0h54m49.70s.
The latitude 51°31'45.48" follows from φ = 180° − ζ − δ (≈0).
The values ≈9.58543, 9.57626, 9.56288 and 9.54323 match the log cos(h/2) column.

transcription_corrections: The star is β Cephei (written as curly ϐ), not ι Cephei. RA 21h26m and Dec +69°44' in 1813 fit β Cep (Alfirk), observed at lower culmination.
The apparent declination of β Cep is 69°44'19.09" (30.38−11.96+0.67), not 19.69; the sum 128°28'14.52" confirms 19.09.
'C.Z. 1. 1. 37.2' means a clock culmination time of 1h1m37.2s for Polaris (upper culmination).
'C.S(φ+δ)' is cosec(φ+δ), i.e. complement of log sin.
The Polaris declination's first line has overwritten digits; it reads 88°18'41.66" (consistent with the result 41.53).
The first hour angle is 134°42'57" (digit overwritten), consistent with 8h58m51.8s.
